Administrator, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
Re: Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs, CMS–0062–P 
Dear Administrator Oz,  
The HIMSS Electronic Health Record (EHR) Association appreciates CMS’s continued leadership in 
advancing interoperability and reducing administrative burden by modernizing prior authorization 
processes. We support the overarching goals of this proposed rule, including expanding electronic prior 
authorization capabilities for drugs, advancing standards-based interoperability, and reducing manual 
workflows that contribute to delays in patient care and administrative inefficiencies across the 
healthcare system. 
The EHR Association represents nearly 30 health IT developer companies whose technologies support 
the vast majority of hospitals and ambulatory providers across the United States. Many of our members 
have been actively engaged in the development, implementation, testing, and deployment of electronic 
prior authorization capabilities, including participation in industry initiatives involving the Da Vinci 
implementation guides, NCPDP standards, and CMS interoperability programs. As such, we strongly 
support the industry’s movement toward more automated, standards-based prior authorization 
workflows. 
At the same time, successful implementation of electronic prior authorization requires careful 
coordination among payers, providers, EHR developers, pharmacy systems, intermediaries, standards 
development organizations, and government agencies. Experience from prior interoperability initiatives 
has consistently shown that the value of new requirements is maximized when all stakeholders can 
advance together with mature standards, realistic implementation timelines, and readily available 
testing infrastructure. 
The EHR Association remains committed to working collaboratively with CMS, ONC, standards 
development organizations, payers, providers, and other stakeholders to advance electronic prior  
 
 
 
 
2 
authorization and interoperability in ways that reduce burden, improve efficiency, and ultimately 
support better patient care.  
Our specific comments follow. 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Leigh Burchell 
Chair, EHR Association 
Altera Digital Health 
Stephanie Jamison 
Vice Chair, EHR Association 
Greenway Health 
 
HIMSS EHR Association Executive Committee 
 
 
Kayla Frederickson 
Oracle Health 
Danielle Friend 
Epic 
 
 
Steve Holt, JD 
PointClickCare 
Michelle Knighton 
NextGen Healthcare 
 
Ida Mantashi 
Modernizing Medicine 
Shari Medina, MD 
Harris Computer/MEDHOST 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Established in 2004, the Electronic Health Record (EHR) Association is comprised of 27 companies that supply the vast majority of EHRs to physicians’ practices 
and hospitals across the United States. The EHR Association operates on the premise that the rapid, widespread adoption of EHRs will help improve the quality of 
patient care as well as the productivity and sustainability of the healthcare system as a key enabler of healthcare transformation. The EHR Association and its 
members are committed to supporting safe healthcare delivery, fostering continued innovation, and operating with high integrity in the market for our users and 
their patients and families. The EHR Association is a partner of HIMSS. For more information, visit www.ehra.org.  
 
3 
Electronic Health Record Association 
Comments on the Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule  
(CMS-0062-P)
 
Overall 
Throughout these comments, the EHR Association encourages CMS to continue balancing the desire for 
rapid interoperability advancement with the practical realities of implementation. In particular, we urge 
CMS to preserve flexibility where standards and implementation guides continue to evolve, avoid 
prematurely locking the industry into versions that have not yet achieved broad deployment experience, 
and ensure that requirements remain aligned with the availability of testing tools and real-world 
implementation readiness. 
We also encourage continued coordination between CMS and ONC. The policies proposed in this rule 
intersect directly with health IT certification requirements, implementation guide adoption, and future 
standards advancement activities. Alignment across federal programs will help reduce unnecessary 
complexity, minimize duplication of effort, and promote more consistent adoption across the healthcare 
ecosystem. 
In addition, CMS should ensure that the policies proposed in CMS-0062-P are aligned with related 
interoperability and electronic prior authorization requirements across other CMS rulemaking, including 
the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program requirements adopted through the Inpatient 
Prospective Payment System (IPPS) rulemaking and corresponding requirements for eligible clinicians 
through the Physician Fee Schedule (PFS). Stakeholders should not face differing definitions, 
implementation expectations, transaction requirements, or timelines across programs that are intended 
to advance the same electronic prior authorization workflows. Consistent policy direction across CMS 
programs will improve implementation efficiency, reduce burden, and promote more successful 
adoption by payers, providers, and health IT developers. 
CRD/DTR/PAS Modular Support 
The EHR Association supports CMS’s proposal to allow the use of one or more of the Da Vinci Coverage 
Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), or Prior Authorization 
Support (PAS) capabilities in support of the Prior Authorization API through 2027. This flexibility reflects 
the reality that implementation and adoption of these capabilities will occur at varying rates across the 
healthcare ecosystem and will support continued advancement of electronic prior authorization 
workflows. 
Bonus Year 
The EHR Association supports the IPPS NPRM proposal for a bonus year for successful Prior 
Authorization API transactions using one or more of the CRD, DTR, or PAS capabilities. We also support 
the goal of aligning stakeholders on version 2.2 of the applicable implementation guides beginning 
October 1, 2027, for payers and January 1, 2028, for providers. 
We also discussed at great length the related CMS proposals in the 2027 IPPS NPRM to change the ePA 
measure from requiring that transactions use data from CEHRT to requiring the actual use of CEHRT 
 
4 
(e.g., using health IT certified to the CRD, DTR, and/or PAS criteria). Many of our member companies felt 
that the measure should be retained as-is to afford maximum flexibility for earning bonus points in 
2027, given that many ePA implementations are currently on version 2.1 and therefore would not be 
certifiable. However, others felt that it would be contradictory to program principles not to cite 
associated criteria when required to achieve a measure, where such criteria exist. If CMS chooses to 
adopt this change, we stress the importance of CMS and ONC collaborating to accelerate the availability 
of authoritative test tools, enabling reliable certification on version 2.2 as quickly as possible. 
Finally, we strongly encourage CMS and ONC to adjust the current January 1, 2027 payer deadline to July 
1, 2027 for the use of version 2.2 of the standards. Together, these policies would enable 2027 to serve 
as a meaningful year for testing, implementation, and alignment on version 2.2, while advancing the 
adoption of the Prior Authorization API with demonstrable success. 
Versions 
The EHR Association recommends that version 2.0 of the Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS implementation 
guides remain available through January 1, 2028, if certified capabilities are required to achieve a 
successful transaction and qualify for bonus points. Maintaining version 2.0 through January 1, 2028 
would provide stakeholders with a reasonable opportunity to use the certified capabilities available 
while transitioning to newer versions. 
However, if CMS decides to allow successful transactions to be achieved using data from CEHRT rather 
than requiring certified capabilities, the expiration date for version 2.0 of the Da Vinci Prior 
Authorization API guides could reasonably be the effective date of the final rule. 
Using the CDex IG for the Prior Authorization API for exchanging attachments related to prior 
authorization 
While we support the intent and general direction of advancing the Da Vinci CDex Implementation 
Guide (IG) within the prior authorization workflow, we believe requiring support for this capability is 
premature for both payers and providers. Enabling health plans to request additional information from 
providers, in line with the DTR data-collection approach, is a logical future direction. However, there is 
currently insufficient real-world implementation experience with CDex within electronic prior 
authorization workflows to justify requiring its support at this time. 
We note that ONC has proposed including the Da Vinci CDex IG in §170.215 and §170.299, but has not 
proposed adopting it as part of the electronic prior authorization certification criteria in §170.315. We 
support this approach. Accordingly, we believe CMS should encourage use of the CDex IG as the 
preferred method for exchanging additional information related to prior authorization, as stakeholders 
are ready to implement it, but should not require its use in the initial rollout. 
The capability to request and exchange information beyond what is provided through PAS is not critical 
to the initial deployment of electronic prior authorization workflows. However, organizations prepared 
to implement the request and exchange of additional information should utilize the CDex IG, as 
referenced by the PAS IG. This approach will support continued industry experience and contribute to 
the further maturation of CDex for prior authorization use cases. 
 
5 
Proposal to require impacted payers to incorporate coverage and documentation 
requirements into the Prior Authorization API 
While we support the general direction of incorporating drugs covered under a medical benefit into the 
Prior Authorization API workflow, we are concerned that implementation beginning in 2028 would be 
premature. In particular, additional updates to the CRD and sufficient real-world implementation 
experience are needed to ensure that payers can accurately indicate, during the CRD process, whether a 
drug is covered under a medical benefit or a prescription benefit, thereby directing the use of the 
appropriate HL7 FHIR- or NCPDP-based workflow. 
We also note that there is currently no corresponding requirement for healthcare providers through the 
Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program electronic prior authorization measure. Given the need 
for further standards maturation and implementation experience, we recommend that CMS defer 
inclusion of drugs covered under a medical benefit in the Prior Authorization API workflow until at least 
2029 and reassess readiness based on lessons learned from initial implementations. 
Is the rubric to categorize drugs as within the scope of the Prior Authorization API (covered 
under a medical benefit) or within the scope of the NCPDP standards (covered under a 
pharmacy benefit) based on the system through which the claims are processed applicable to 
and appropriate for all or most state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs? 
As noted above, we believe CRD is the appropriate mechanism for determining whether a drug should 
be processed through the HL7 FHIR-based Prior Authorization API workflow or through the NCPDP-
based workflow. Specifically, the payer should be able to indicate through the CRD response whether 
prior authorization is required and, if so, whether the transaction should proceed via the applicable 
FHIR- or NCPDP-based process. 
However, the current version of the CRD does not sufficiently define how this information should be 
conveyed consistently across health plans. Additional clarification and standards development are 
needed to ensure interoperable implementation and avoid variability in payer responses. We therefore 
recommend that this capability be addressed in a future version of CRD before CMS incorporates it into 
program requirements. 
The proposal to require impacted payers to report all API endpoints to CMS, in the form of an 
Endpoint Resource, as defined by an unexpired version of the FHIR standard adopted in 45 
CFR 170.215(a), including, if multiple, appropriate use cases for each. 
We support the proposed requirement for payers to report all API endpoints to CMS. We also strongly 
recommend that health plans publish their API endpoints and provide references to relevant 
documentation, implementation guidance, and test environments on their public websites. When a 
provider, developer, or other stakeholder is seeking information for a specific health plan, it is beneficial 
to locate it directly on the health plan’s website rather than relying solely on a centralized directory. 
Accordingly, while the National Provider Directory may serve as a valuable centralized resource once it 
includes health plans, health plans should also maintain this information within their own public-facing 
resources to improve accessibility and facilitate implementation. 
 
 
6 
Certification of Payer API Technology 
The EHR Association believes it is premature to require mandatory certification of payer API technology, 
given the ongoing development of current standards (as described in more detail in our comments 
above on the Bonus Year). The Association shares CMS's goal of ensuring that payer APIs conform to 
required standards and operate reliably but does not believe that applying ONC certification to payer 
API technology is an effective way to achieve that goal at this time. Rather, such a requirement should 
start with version 2.2 of the guides, when everyone can align on a common version. This approach 
reflects the fact that the electronic prior authorization space is rapidly evolving and needs flexibility to 
move quickly. 
In its place, we recommend three approaches to advance standardized interoperability. First, CMS 
should work with ONC to ensure that, in its rulemaking, the version requirements are aligned for payers, 
providers, and health IT developers certifying. Second, CMS should work with ONC to make high-quality 
testing tools available at least 18 months before compliance deadlines. A recurring obstacle in prior 
authorization API adoption has been the lag between when standards are finalized and when 
implementers can actually test against them, and reliable, publicly available testing infrastructure would 
do more to drive conformance than a certification mandate. Third, CMS should lead by example, 
implementing the required standards in its own prior authorization workflows early in the compliance 
window so that providers have ample time to test in advance of the deadlines. 
We do note our opinion (driven by precedent) that absent a clear market incentive, voluntary 
certification by payers is unlikely to gain traction. Therefore, while we believe payer certification is not 
appropriate for 2027, we suggest that as the standards development process reaches certain maturity 
milestones, payer certification requirements should be equal and commensurate to those imposed upon 
EHRs and would be appropriately required as early as 2028. Setting a lower bar for payers causes 
industry delay and higher costs, so parity of requirements is something we would support at the 
appropriate time. 
The proposal to define prior authorization to mean transmissions described in 45 CFR 
162.1301(a) used by health care providers to obtain authorization for health care, and 
transmissions described in 45 CFR 162.1301(c) used by health plans to respond to such 
requests (see section II.H.2. of this proposed rule). The alternative proposal to adopt the FHIR 
standards of this proposed rule for all “referral certification and authorization transactions” 
described in 45 CFR 162.1301 (see section II.H.2. of this proposed rule). 
The Association supports the proposed updates to these definitions, which would enable the use of the 
HL7 FHIR-based prior authorization implementation guides proposed in this rule. Clarifying the 
definitions in this manner will help support consistent implementation and adoption of electronic prior 
authorization workflows across the healthcare ecosystem. 
The proposal to modify the current operating rules that are associated with the “eligibility for 
a health plan” transaction to exclude prior authorization-related transmissions (see section 
II.H.5. of this proposed rule). 
We support the proposed modification to the operating rules governing eligibility for a health plan 
transaction to exclude prior authorization-related transmissions. This change will help facilitate the 
adoption and use of the HL7 FHIR-based prior authorization implementation guides proposed in this rule 
 
7 
and provide greater clarity regarding the appropriate standards and workflows for electronic prior 
authorization transactions. 
Whether adopting the FHIR standards for prior authorization transmissions and retaining the 
currently adopted X12N transaction standards for other referral certification transmission use 
cases would increase burden on HIPAA covered entities to maintain the ability to conduct 
electronic transactions using two different standards (see section II.H.2. of this proposed 
rule). 
While maintaining support for multiple standards may introduce additional complexity, we believe any 
such burden should be viewed as transitional. Given the current limited adoption of the X12 standards 
for these use cases and the opportunity for FHIR-based approaches to be more deeply integrated into 
providers' clinical and administrative workflows, we expect the industry to increasingly move toward 
FHIR-based prior authorization transactions. As adoption grows, the need to maintain multiple 
standards should diminish. 
Should HHS adopt any later versions of the proposed standards, including more recent 
versions that are currently available and versions that may become available between the 
publication of the proposed and final rules (see section II.H.6. of this proposed rule)? 
At this time, we believe version 2.2 is the appropriate version to adopt as the common industry target 
for 2028, and we strongly encourage all stakeholders to begin transitioning to version 2.2 as soon as 
reasonably possible. Achieving broad alignment on version 2.2 will require sufficient implementation 
time, and as discussed earlier, relieving payers of the current January 1, 2027 deadline will be an 
important step in enabling stakeholders to focus their efforts on a coordinated transition rather than 
implementing intermediate versions solely to meet existing regulatory timelines. 
At the same time, stakeholders should expect continued evolution of these specifications. A subsequent 
version is likely to become available in 2027 and should incorporate lessons learned from real-world 
implementation of version 2.2. The SVAP process can then be leveraged to make that newer version 
available to early adopters while the industry gains implementation experience and evaluates the 
impact of any changes. 
Depending on the scope of changes introduced in a future version, whether version 2.3, 3.0, or another 
release, CMS should establish a reasonable timeline for broader regulatory adoption through a future 
rulemaking cycle. Alternatively, CMS could follow the approach used for other standards, including the 
FHIR US Core Implementation Guide, where a subsequent version becomes the next regulatory baseline 
after sufficient implementation experience has been gained. In either case, version 2.2 should be viewed 
as an important milestone rather than the final destination, with future versions continuing to advance 
the specifications based on industry experience and lessons learned. 
Would amending or removing the direct data entry exception lead to greater adoption of 
electronic transaction standards or would it perversely incentivize HIPAA-covered entities to 
move to fully manual transactions? 
While removing the direct data entry exception may be an appropriate future consideration, we believe 
doing so now would be premature. The industry has not yet gained sufficient practical experience with 
 
8 
the Prior Authorization API and the associated electronic prior authorization workflows to fully 
understand the implications of eliminating the exception. 
We encourage CMS to revisit this issue in a future rulemaking cycle once end-to-end electronic prior 
authorization workflows are more broadly implemented, established, and mature. At that point, CMS 
will be better positioned to evaluate whether removal of the exception would promote greater adoption 
of electronic transaction standards without creating unintended consequences. 
How have existing statutes and regulations, within CMS's purview, shaped your cybersecurity 
strategies, and what changes or additions by CMS would enhance your ability to safeguard 
health information? 
Existing federal privacy and security requirements have played an important role in shaping 
cybersecurity strategies across the healthcare ecosystem. As CMS considers future cybersecurity 
policies, several overarching principles should guide any new or modified requirements. 
● Security and Privacy Should Be Addressed Together - Security and privacy are deeply 
interconnected and should be treated as complementary components of patient data 
protection. Requirements that address these concepts in isolation can create organizational silos 
and unintended gaps in accountability. CMS should continue to recognize that protecting health 
information is simultaneously a privacy and a security responsibility and reflect that principle in 
future policy development. 
● Policies Should Prioritize Risk Reduction While Remaining Achievable - Cybersecurity 
requirements should be driven by the goal of reducing risk and protecting patients, rather than 
by short-term cost considerations alone. The consequences of inadequate cybersecurity, 
including operational disruption, loss of patient trust, financial harm, and potential impacts on 
patient care, can far exceed the cost of implementing reasonable safeguards. CMS should focus 
on identifying meaningful security outcomes while ensuring that providers of varying sizes and 
resources have practical pathways to achieve them. 
● Regulatory Development Should Be Informed by Operational Expertise - Effective 
cybersecurity policy depends on a clear understanding of how health IT systems are 
implemented, maintained, and used in real-world healthcare environments. Continued 
engagement with providers, health IT developers, cybersecurity practitioners, and other 
stakeholders throughout the rulemaking process will help ensure that future requirements are 
technically feasible, operationally practical, and aligned with current cybersecurity practices. 
CMS should continue investing in internal cybersecurity expertise and leveraging stakeholder 
input to inform policy development. 
What are the most significant cybersecurity challenges faced by health care organizations, 
providers, and entities—including hospitals, clinics, state Medicaid and Children's Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) agencies, commercial plans, and other health care stakeholders—in 
securing patient data and preventing and recovering from cyberattacks?  
Cybersecurity challenges across the healthcare ecosystem are multifaceted and span organizational, 
financial, workforce, cultural, and technical dimensions. 
 
9 
● Organizational - Cybersecurity is often treated as an IT responsibility rather than an enterprise 
risk management issue. Clinical and executive leadership may not become fully engaged until 
after a significant incident has occurred, limiting organizations’ ability to proactively manage 
cybersecurity risks. 
● Financial - Cybersecurity programs are frequently underfunded, particularly among smaller 
hospitals, rural providers, and safety-net organizations. Investments in cybersecurity are often 
deferred because their benefits may not be immediately visible, despite the substantial 
financial, operational, and patient safety risks associated with cyber incidents. 
● Workforce - Many healthcare organizations struggle to recruit and retain qualified cybersecurity 
professionals. As a result, cybersecurity responsibilities are often assigned to general IT 
personnel who may lack the specialized training, expertise, or resources necessary to effectively 
manage evolving cyber threats. 
● Cultural - Healthcare organizations appropriately prioritize patient care and operational 
continuity. However, security controls that introduce additional steps or workflow changes can 
face resistance unless they are supported by leadership and clearly connected to broader 
organizational priorities, including patient safety and operational resilience. 
● Structural Complexity - The healthcare ecosystem depends on a complex network of 
interconnected stakeholders, including providers, health IT developers, clearinghouses, billing 
services, medical device manufacturers, cloud service providers, and other third parties. Each 
connection represents a potential attack vector, while security responsibilities across these 
relationships are often not clearly defined. As a result, the healthcare sector faces a particularly 
large and challenging supply chain attack surface. 
What are the most effective current practices, technologies, and innovative strategies for 
preventing, detecting, and responding to cyberattacks in the health care sector? Should CMS 
propose any of these practices or strategies as regulatory requirements within its purview? 
Fragmented and inconsistent requirements across federal agencies substantially increase compliance 
burdens for EHR developers and healthcare providers without producing proportionate improvements 
in security outcomes. The EHR Association therefore urges CMS to avoid establishing cybersecurity 
requirements that diverge from existing industry standards. 
When establishing new requirements, CMS should avoid one-size-fits-all mandates. The healthcare 
ecosystem is highly diverse, encompassing large health systems with dedicated security teams, small 
rural practices with a single administrator, and everything in between. Prescriptive requirements that 
may be feasible for large organizations can be unachievable for smaller entities and may ultimately 
produce compliance theater rather than meaningful improvements in security. For organizations to 
adopt security practices appropriate to their size, resources, risk profile, and operational environment, 
requirements should focus on the security outcomes to be achieved rather than prescribe the specific 
technical means of achieving them.  
Some foundational principles, however, should be broadly applicable across the healthcare ecosystem, 
including: 
 
10 
● Asset Management - Asset management is a foundational cybersecurity practice, not an 
advanced capability. Organizations cannot protect what they cannot identify or inventory. A 
continuously maintained inventory of hardware, software, systems, and data assets, with clearly 
designated owners, is a prerequisite for nearly every other security control. 
● Clinical Workforce Education - Clinicians and their support staff remain among the most 
frequently exploited entry points for cyberattacks, not because they are careless or incapable, 
but because they often lack sufficient training and preparation. Cybersecurity education should 
be role-specific, clinically relevant, and framed as a patient safety responsibility rather than an 
annual compliance exercise. 
What are the major challenges and barriers that health care organizations face in 
implementing robust cybersecurity measures? How have health care organizations overcome 
these challenges and barriers? 
One significant challenge facing healthcare organizations is effectively sharing and acting on 
cybersecurity threat intelligence across the sector. Cyber threats often target multiple organizations 
using similar tactics, making timely information sharing an important component of an effective 
cybersecurity strategy. 
The Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center (Health-ISAC) provides an important mechanism for 
healthcare organizations to access shared threat intelligence and to benefit from their peers' 
experiences. However, the full potential of threat intelligence sharing is significantly constrained by 
liability concerns. Organizations may be reluctant to share detailed information about cybersecurity 
incidents for fear that such disclosures could be used against them in enforcement actions or litigation 
or could result in reputational harm. This chilling effect can limit both the quality and specificity of 
information shared, reducing the effectiveness of collaborative defense efforts across the sector. 
CMS, in coordination with other federal partners, should explore mechanisms to provide meaningful 
liability protections for the good-faith sharing of cybersecurity incident information within trusted 
information-sharing communities. Strengthening these protections would encourage more robust 
information sharing, improve situational awareness across the healthcare ecosystem, and ultimately 
enhance the sector’s collective cybersecurity resilience. 
What are some best practices for cybersecurity training? How can CMS promote best 
practices in cybersecurity? 
Effective cybersecurity training should extend beyond annual compliance-based education and focus on 
preparing personnel to recognize, prevent, and respond to real-world threats. Cybersecurity training 
programs should include: 
● Role-Specific Training - Training should be tailored to the specific risks and responsibilities 
associated with each workforce role. Clinicians, administrative staff, executives, and IT 
personnel face distinct cybersecurity threats and should receive training tailored to their day-to-
day responsibilities. 
 
11 
● Phishing Simulations - Organizations should conduct regular phishing simulations accompanied 
by constructive feedback and targeted remediation. Repeated failures to follow established 
cybersecurity practices should be addressed through appropriate accountability measures. 
● Tabletop Exercises - Regular tabletop exercises should involve both clinical and operational 
leadership to ensure that organizations are prepared to respond effectively to cybersecurity 
incidents while maintaining continuity of patient care. 
● Outcome-Based Measurement - Organizations should evaluate the effectiveness of training 
programs by measuring outcomes such as phishing susceptibility rates, incident reporting rates, 
and response times. These metrics should be regularly reviewed by organizational leadership 
and used to drive continuous improvement. 
CMS can promote these best practices by emphasizing outcome-based cybersecurity expectations, 
supporting the dissemination of educational resources, and encouraging organizations to adopt training 
programs that are tailored to their workforce, risk profile, and operational environment. 
In the broader context of ransomware attacks, how do offsite backups, redundant systems, 
and security protocols enhance health care resiliency? Are there other approaches, tools, or 
policies, within CMS's purview, that would enhance resiliency following an attack? 
When a ransomware attack or other cyber incident disrupts a provider’s systems, the operational 
emergency is often compounded by an acute cash flow crisis. If claims cannot be processed during a 
system outage, providers may face an immediate and severe reduction in revenue at precisely the 
moment they are also incurring extraordinary remediation and recovery costs. 
Ensuring that providers can meet payroll and sustain patient care during a cyber recovery period is one 
of the most direct and impactful actions CMS could take to strengthen healthcare system resilience. 
Financial destabilization should not be an inevitable consequence of being the victim of a cyberattack. 
We recommend that CMS establish a formal policy to provide interim payments based on an 
organization’s average daily claims volume during a qualifying cybersecurity disruption. CMS would need 
to define clear criteria for qualifying disruptions and establish a streamlined process for affected 
providers to attest to their status. Once systems are restored, CMS should also provide a clear 
reconciliation process to address any overpayments or underpayments. 
Additional measures that CMS and other HHS agencies should consider include: 
● Tested, Air-Gapped, Immutable Backups - Ransomware actors frequently target backup 
systems, and online backups connected to the primary network may offer limited protection. 
CMS and HHS should identify opportunities within their authority to encourage or require 
demonstrated, tested offline backup capabilities. 
● Incident Response and Recovery Exercises - Organizations should conduct exercises that go 
beyond tabletop discussions and include actual execution of downtime procedures, with 
recovery timelines validated against real system restoration capabilities. These exercises are the 
cybersecurity equivalent of a fire drill and should be normalized accordingly. 
 
12 
● Resilience Measurement - CMS and HHS should consider establishing resilience metrics that 
assess outcomes rather than prescriptive controls. Relevant metrics could include how quickly 
critical systems can be restored, how long an organization can operate in downtime mode, and 
whether paper-based fallback procedures have been tested within the prior 12 months. Paper-
based operational testing remains underutilized and should be incorporated into formal 
resilience expectations. Requiring organizations to answer these questions would drive more 
meaningful testing and strengthen operational preparedness. 
How do the enrollment and implementation processes for health care clearinghouses affect 
the health care industry's ability to remain resilient? How could this be improved? 
Under current processes, enrolling with a new clearinghouse and successfully establishing electronic 
claims submission and payment exchange can take several weeks. The administrative burden of 
onboarding effectively prevents providers from switching to a backup clearinghouse within the 
timeframe required in a crisis. As a result, when a primary clearinghouse experiences a major outage or 
becomes the victim of a cyberattack, as occurred with Change Healthcare, providers may be left without 
a viable alternative for claims submission and payment processing. 
Reducing friction in clearinghouse enrollment, testing, and activation would improve redundancy and 
resilience across the healthcare payment ecosystem. Providers should be able to establish and maintain 
backup clearinghouse relationships that can be activated quickly during a cyber emergency or other 
operational disruption. 
We urge CMS to explore opportunities to streamline the enrollment and implementation processes for 
establishing clearinghouse relationships. Particular attention should be given to reducing barriers that 
prevent providers from rapidly activating backup clearinghouses when their primary claims-processing 
pathway becomes unavailable. 
What perspectives, needs, barriers, and challenges specifically affect the ability of health care 
providers in small and rural practices, who participate in health care programs within CMS's 
authority, to improve their cybersecurity preparedness, response, recovery, and resiliency? 
Small and rural providers are not simply smaller versions of large health systems. They operate in 
fundamentally different resource environments, and uniform cybersecurity requirements often fail to 
account for those differences. Common challenges include the lack of dedicated security personnel, 
heavy reliance on EHR developers and managed service providers, limited ability to independently 
assess developers' security practices, constrained financial resources, aging infrastructure, and 
unreliable broadband connectivity, which can undermine the effectiveness of cloud-based security tools. 
CMS should recognize these realities when considering cybersecurity policies and requirements. 
Measures that may be appropriate for large health systems can be impractical or unattainable for 
smaller providers and may divert resources away from higher-value security activities. 
Several approaches could help improve cybersecurity preparedness, response, recovery, and resilience 
among small and rural providers: 
● Tiered Implementation Models - Requirements for small and rural providers should focus on 
the highest-impact and most achievable security practices, including multifactor authentication, 
 
13 
basic asset inventory, tested backups, and documented downtime procedures. The Health 
Industry Cybersecurity Practices (HICP) framework developed pursuant to Section 405(d) of the 
Cybersecurity Act of 2015 provides a useful foundation for a tiered approach. 
● Direct Financial and Technical Assistance - CMS should explore opportunities to support 
baseline cybersecurity improvements for under-resourced providers through Medicare and 
Medicaid program authorities. Technical assistance programs modeled on the Quality 
Improvement Organization framework, including security assessments and remediation support, 
could provide a practical and effective means to improve cybersecurity readiness. 
● Regional Shared-Service Security Models - CMS should encourage and, where possible, support 
models that enable smaller providers to collectively access cybersecurity capabilities that would 
otherwise be out of reach, such as security operations centers, threat intelligence services, and 
incident response resources. Shared-service approaches can improve cybersecurity resilience 
while reducing costs for individual providers.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** HIMSS Electronic Health Record (EHR) Association; signed by Leigh Burchell, Chair, and Stephanie Jamison, Vice Chair, with executive committee members from EHR developers.
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor; Professional Association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents 27-30 health IT developer companies supplying the vast majority of EHRs to U.S. physician practices and hospitals; members participate in Da Vinci IG, NCPDP, and CMS interoperability implementation and testing.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The EHR Association supports CMS's goals for electronic prior authorization and drug PA modernization, but urges careful alignment with ONC certification, testing tools, and standards maturity. It recommends flexibility for CRD/DTR/PAS modular support, alignment on version 2.2, deferral of medical-benefit drug PA API requirements until at least 2029, public payer endpoints, phased payer API certification, and a cautious approach to CDex, direct data entry, and cybersecurity mandates.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL/RFIs.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 45 CFR 170.215; 45 CFR 170.299; 45 CFR 170.315; 45 CFR 162.1301; references to IPPS and PFS rulemaking.
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR; Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS; Da Vinci CDex; NCPDP standards; X12N; CEHRT; SVAP; FHIR US Core.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Federal alignment and implementation flexibility**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Requirements intersect with health IT certification, implementation guide adoption, testing infrastructure, and multiple CMS programs. Inconsistent timelines and definitions would increase complexity.
- **Specific request:** Align CMS, ONC, IPPS, and PFS requirements and preserve flexibility while standards continue to evolve.

**Topic 2: CRD/DTR/PAS modular support and bonus year**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Adoption of CRD, DTR, and PAS will vary by stakeholder; 2027 should be a meaningful testing and alignment year.
- **Specific request:** Allow one or more CRD/DTR/PAS capabilities through 2027, support the IPPS bonus year, align stakeholders on version 2.2, and move the January 1, 2027 payer version 2.2 deadline to July 1, 2027.

**Topic 3: Versioning of Da Vinci PA guides**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Many implementations use version 2.1 and may not yet be certifiable; version 2.2 should be the common industry target but needs transition time.
- **Specific request:** Keep version 2.0 available through January 1, 2028 if certified capabilities are required; use SVAP and future rulemaking for later versions.

**Topic 4: CDex for prior authorization attachments**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CDex may be useful for additional information exchange, but there is insufficient real-world PA workflow experience to require it.
- **Specific request:** Encourage CDex as a preferred optional method when ready, but do not require it in the initial rollout.

**Topic 5: Medical-benefit drug PA API and benefit routing**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** CRD is the right mechanism for distinguishing FHIR vs NCPDP workflows, but current CRD does not consistently define how payers convey benefit classification and routing.
- **Specific request:** Defer medical-benefit drug PA API inclusion until at least 2029 and address benefit routing in a future CRD version before requiring it.

**Topic 6: API endpoints and payer API certification**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Endpoint reporting improves discoverability, but health plans should also publish endpoints and documentation on their own public websites. Mandatory payer API certification is premature without aligned standards and test tools.
- **Specific request:** Require payer endpoint reporting to CMS and public payer website documentation; provide test tools at least 18 months before deadlines; consider payer certification beginning with version 2.2 and potentially as early as 2028.

**Topic 7: HIPAA PA standards and X12 coexistence**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Updating definitions to support FHIR-based PA workflows is appropriate; maintaining X12 for other referral certification uses may create temporary complexity but should diminish as FHIR adoption grows.
- **Specific request:** Finalize definition updates and operating rule modifications while treating dual-standard burden as transitional.

**Topic 8: Direct data entry exception**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Removing the exception now could create unintended consequences because end-to-end PA API workflows are not mature.
- **Specific request:** Revisit the exception in a future rulemaking after broader implementation.

**Topic 9: Cybersecurity and resiliency RFIs**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Cybersecurity requirements should be risk-based, outcome-focused, aligned with existing standards, and feasible for smaller and rural providers.
- **Specific request:** Address privacy and security together; avoid one-size-fits-all mandates; promote asset management, workforce education, MFA, backups, incident response, threat intelligence protections, interim payments during cyber disruptions, and clearinghouse resilience.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1/S18/S37:** Supports mandatory IG movement in principle but stresses implementation flexibility, modular CRD/DTR/PAS support, and testing readiness.
- **S2/S3/S60-S65:** Recommends version 2.2 as the common industry target for 2028, transitional availability for older versions, and SVAP/future rulemaking for later versions.
- **S12/S15/S21:** Supports medical-benefit drug PA direction but says implementation beginning in 2028 is premature; recommends deferral until at least 2029 and improved CRD benefit-routing standards.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports CMS endpoint reporting and recommends payer public websites also include endpoints, documentation, guidance, and test environments.
- **S44-S56:** Supports FHIR-based PA definition updates and operating rule changes; views X12 coexistence as transitional; recommends version 2.2 and sufficient time.
- **S54/S55:** Opposes mandatory payer API certification in 2027; recommends aligned version requirements, public testing tools 18 months before deadlines, and possible payer certification after maturity milestones.
- **S66-S82:** Provides extensive cybersecurity and resiliency RFI responses focused on outcome-based security, role-specific training, ransomware recovery, clearinghouse redundancy, rural/small provider support, and liability protections for threat sharing.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Preserve flexibility as IGs and standards evolve.
2. Align CMS and ONC rulemaking, certification, test tools, and program timelines.
3. Allow modular CRD/DTR/PAS support through 2027.
4. Use version 2.2 as the common target, but avoid premature cutoff of earlier usable versions where certification timing requires them.
5. Do not require CDex in the initial ePA rollout; encourage it as ready.
6. Defer medical-benefit drug PA API inclusion until at least 2029.
7. Improve CRD standards for medical vs pharmacy benefit routing before making drug routing mandatory.
8. Require payer endpoint reporting and encourage payer public website publication.
9. Make authoritative testing tools available at least 18 months before compliance deadlines.
10. Delay mandatory payer API certification until standards and testing tools are mature.
11. Finalize HIPAA PA definition and operating rule updates supporting FHIR PA.
12. Revisit direct data entry exception only after workflows are mature.
13. Use cybersecurity requirements that are achievable, risk-based, and coordinated with existing standards.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Premature standards lock-in; insufficient testing tools; immature CDex and CRD drug-routing use cases; misalignment across CMS/ONC programs; premature payer API certification; overprescriptive cybersecurity requirements.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Duplicative effort, implementation failures, workflow disruption, inability to certify, payer variability, increased provider and vendor burden, and security compliance burdens without proportional risk reduction.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Version misalignment, lack of authoritative test tools, limited real-world experience, EHR certification timing, payer/provider readiness gaps, clearinghouse onboarding delays, and small/rural provider resource limits.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Represents 27-30 EHR developer companies supporting the vast majority of U.S. hospitals and ambulatory providers.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Relies primarily on industry implementation experience and federal program alignment rather than external studies.
- **Examples provided:** Current ePA implementations on version 2.1; CDex not included in ePA certification criteria; Change Healthcare-type clearinghouse disruption; need for interim payments after cyber incidents.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** EHR developers, payers, providers, hospitals, ambulatory practices, clearinghouses, pharmacy systems, SDOs, CMS, ONC, small and rural providers.
- **Economic implications:** Poor alignment or premature requirements could increase implementation cost and rework; testing tools and aligned versions could reduce waste.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible with version alignment, mature test tools, phased certification, and deferral of immature drug-routing requirements.
- **Patient care impact:** Better ePA integration can reduce delays; rushed or fragmented implementation could produce unreliable workflows and delays.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive but cautious.
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, collaborative.
- **Priority level:** High.
